chapter.name: Particulate Nature of Matter
chapter.blurb: How matter is made up of extremely small constituent particles held together by interparticle attraction; how the strength of this attraction and the spacing between particles differ in solids, liquids and gases, giving each state its own shape, volume, compressibility and melting or boiling point; and how the constant motion of particles, faster with more heat, makes a dissolved colour or a smell spread through a liquid or a gas.

scope_in.item: Activity 7.1 (grinding chalk): repeated breaking and grinding still gives chalk, a physical change, showing matter is made of extremely small constituent particles too small to see even under an ordinary microscope

Activity 7.2 (dissolving sugar): water tastes sweet throughout only after stirring dissolves the sugar completely, even though no sugar particles are visible, because sugar breaks into constituent particles sensed by taste; these particles occupy interparticle spaces between water particles

Interparticle attraction: the forces holding constituent particles together, whose strength depends on the nature of the substance and the interparticle distance, and which decides the physical state of a substance

Solid state (Activity 7.3): solids have a definite shape and volume because particles are tightly packed with strong interparticle attraction, held in fixed positions, able only to vibrate/oscillate, not move past each other

Melting point: the minimum temperature at which a solid melts to a liquid at atmospheric pressure, reached when vibrations become vigorous enough for particles to leave their positions; Table 7.1 melting points of ice (0 degrees C), urea (133 degrees C) and iron (1538 degrees C); weak interparticle forces give low melting points, strong forces give high melting points

Liquid state (Activity 7.4): water takes the shape of whichever of three differently shaped containers it is poured into but its volume stays at 200 mL in each, so liquids have no fixed shape but a definite volume, because liquid particles are free to move but only within a limited space

Liquid interparticle attraction: a finger can move through water without cutting it permanently and its position is restored afterwards, showing liquid interparticle attraction is slightly weaker than in solids but still strong enough to keep particles close together

Boiling point and evaporation: the temperature at which a liquid boils and turns to vapour at atmospheric pressure; at the boiling point vapour forms fast, at the surface and within the liquid (seen as bubbles); evaporation happens more slowly, only at the surface, at any temperature

Gaseous state (Activity 7.5, smoke between gas jars, and the iodine vapour alternative): a gas spreads to fill the entire available space and takes the shape of its container, because gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible interparticle attraction, so gases have no fixed shape or volume
Fluids: liquids and gases are together called fluids because both flow and do not retain a fixed shape, unlike solids

Compressibility (Activity 7.6, syringe): a gas's volume can be reduced by pushing a plunger because gas particles have a lot of space between them that pressure can reduce, and the gas returns to its original volume when pressure is released; water in the same activity is practically incompressible

Interparticle spaces via dissolving (Activity 7.7): the water level after sugar dissolves completely is lower than the level marked right after adding the (undissolved) sugar, showing there is space between water particles that the dissolved sugar particles come to occupy

Insoluble solids in water: sand does not dissolve; its particles settle and occupy their own space in the container, increasing the total volume, unlike sugar which occupies the interparticle spaces of water
Interparticle spacing in solids: despite close packing, some space is left between particles in a solid, and this space contains nothing at all, not air

Movement of particles in a liquid (Activity 7.8, potassium permanganate in water): pink streaks spread from the grain until the whole water turns uniformly pink because water particles are in constant motion, pulling particles out of the grain and spreading them through the liquid; insoluble substances like sand are held together too strongly for water particles to pull out

Effect of temperature on particle movement: potassium permanganate spreads fastest in hot water, less quickly at room temperature, and slowest in ice-cold water, showing particle movement increases when heat is provided

Movement of particles in air (Activity 7.9, incense stick): a fragrance felt only near the stick at first spreads to fill the whole room because air particles are in constant motion and hit the fragrance particles, helping them spread

Thermal energy and physical state: low thermal energy in solids keeps particles close with only vibrations; at the melting point thermal energy overcomes attractive forces enough for particles to leave fixed positions; in a gas, particles have enough energy to overcome attraction and move freely in all directions
Summary comparison of the three states (the 'Let us wrap up' table): interparticle spacing, packing, interparticle attraction and movement of particles compared across solids, liquids and gases

concepts.name: Matter is made up of tiny constituent particles
concepts.description: Repeatedly breaking and grinding chalk, and dissolving sugar in water, show that matter is made of extremely small constituent particles held together by interparticle attraction.
concepts.idea: All matter is made of very small basic particles, too small to see even under an ordinary microscope, called constituent particles, held together by attractive forces called interparticle attraction.
concepts.rule: When a stick of chalk is broken again and again and then ground with a mortar and pestle, the fine powder obtained is still chalk; grinding only reduces the size of each speck, it is a physical change, not a chemical one. This shows that chalk, like sand and clay, is made up of a very large number of extremely small basic units called constituent particles, too small to see even under an ordinary microscope. When two teaspoons of sugar are put into a glass of water and left unstirred, a spoonful from the top layer does not taste sweet; once the water is stirred until the sugar dissolves completely, a spoonful from the top layer does taste sweet, even though no sugar particles can be seen. This is because the sugar has broken up into its constituent particles, which spread through the water and occupy the spaces between the water particles, called interparticle spaces, and can be sensed by taste even though they cannot be seen. The constituent particles of matter are held together by attractive forces called interparticle attractions. The strength of these attractions depends on the nature of the substance and on the distance between the particles; even a slight increase in distance decreases the interparticle force drastically, and the strength of these forces decides the physical state of the substance.
concepts.example: After sugar dissolves completely in water, every part of the water tastes sweet even though no sugar particles can be seen, because the sugar has broken into constituent particles spread through the water.

questions.q: Explain why 'even a slight increase in interparticle distance decreases the interparticle force drastically' is an important idea for understanding why substances exist in different physical states.

questions.q: Design a simple activity, different from grinding chalk or dissolving sugar, that could help show a younger student that matter is made of tiny constituent particles.
questions.a: For example, dissolving a spoon of salt in water and tasting it after stirring, or crushing a biscuit repeatedly until it becomes a fine powder that still tastes and smells like biscuit, showing the substance is unchanged but broken into smaller and smaller particles.

concepts.name: Particle arrangement in solids and melting point
concepts.description: In solids, particles are tightly packed with strong interparticle attraction, giving a definite shape and volume; heating vibrates particles until the solid melts at its melting point.
concepts.idea: Solids have a definite shape and volume because their particles are tightly packed by strong interparticle attraction and can only vibrate about a fixed position; heating weakens this attraction until the solid melts at its melting point.
concepts.rule: Objects such as an iron nail, a piece of rock salt, a stone, a piece of wood, a key and a piece of aluminium are all solids: they have a definite shape and a definite volume. This is because, in solids, the particles are tightly packed and the interparticle attractions are very strong. These strong forces hold the particles in fixed positions, preventing them from moving freely; the particles can only move to and fro about their positions, called vibrating or oscillating, but cannot move past each other. When a solid is heated, its particles vibrate more vigorously. A stage is reached when these vibrations become so vigorous that the particles start leaving their fixed positions; the interparticle forces of attraction weaken and the solid converts into the liquid state. The minimum temperature at which a solid melts to become a liquid at atmospheric pressure is called its melting point. Some solids have weak interparticle forces of attraction, so their melting points are low, while others have strong attractive forces and high melting points; for example, ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, urea melts at 133 degrees Celsius, and iron melts at 1538 degrees Celsius.
concepts.example: Ice has a low melting point of 0 degrees Celsius because the interparticle forces holding its particles together are comparatively weak, while iron has a very high melting point of 1538 degrees Celsius because its interparticle forces are very strong.

concepts.name: Particle arrangement in liquids: fixed volume, no fixed shape
concepts.description: Liquids take the shape of their container but keep a fixed volume because their particles are free to move within a limited space; heating a liquid to its boiling point turns it into vapour.
concepts.idea: Liquids have no fixed shape but a definite volume because their particles are free to move within a limited space and are held by interparticle attraction slightly weaker than in solids; at the boiling point, particles gain enough energy to escape into the gaseous state.
concepts.rule: When 200 mL of water is poured in turn into three containers, A, B and C, of different shapes, the water takes the shape of whichever container it is in, but its level always stays at 200 mL. This shows liquids do not have a fixed shape and take the shape of the container they are kept in, because the particles of a liquid are free to move; but the volume of the liquid stays the same in every container, so liquids have a definite volume. This happens because the particles of a liquid can move freely, but only within a limited space. Moving a finger through water temporarily displaces the water without cutting it permanently, and the water's position is restored once the finger is removed; this shows that in liquids, the interparticle attractions are slightly weaker than in solids, but still strong enough to keep the particles close together. When a liquid is heated, a stage comes when it starts boiling; the temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour at atmospheric pressure is called its boiling point. At the boiling point, the movement of particles becomes so vigorous that they move apart, decreasing the interparticle forces of attraction until the particles can escape from the liquid, forming vapour rapidly both at the surface and within the liquid, seen as bubbles. Vapour also forms more slowly, and only at the surface, at temperatures below the boiling point; this slower process is called evaporation.
concepts.example: Water poured in turn into three differently shaped containers takes a new shape each time but always measures 200 mL, showing that a liquid has no fixed shape but a definite, fixed volume.

concepts.name: Particle arrangement in gases; liquids and gases as fluids
concepts.description: Gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible interparticle attraction, so a gas spreads to fill all the available space and has no fixed shape or volume; liquids and gases together are called fluids.
concepts.idea: A gas has no fixed shape or volume because its particles move freely in all directions with negligible interparticle attraction, spreading to fill whatever space is available; liquids and gases are together called fluids because both flow and take the shape of their container.
concepts.rule: In Activity 7.5, smoke trapped inside Gas Jar A is allowed to pass into Gas Jar B; the smoke spreads out and fills the entire space of Gas Jar B, showing that gases do not have a fixed volume and tend to occupy the entire available space; like liquids, gases also take the shape of the vessel they are in. This happens because the particles in a gas move freely in all directions and the interparticle attractions between them are negligible; as a result, gases have no fixed shape or volume. The same spreading can be shown using iodine vapour released inside a closed gas jar instead of incense-stick smoke. Because both liquids and gases flow and do not retain a fixed shape, they are together classified as fluids, which distinguishes them from solids.
concepts.example: Smoke released inside one gas jar spreads to completely fill a second, connected gas jar, showing that a gas has no fixed volume and occupies all the space available to it.

concepts.name: Interparticle spacing: compressibility and dissolving
concepts.description: A syringe activity shows gases are compressible while water is not, and a sugar-water activity shows there is space between water particles that dissolved particles can occupy; solids too have some interparticle spacing, which contains nothing at all.
concepts.idea: Interparticle spacing explains why a trapped gas can be compressed but water practically cannot, and why the volume of water after dissolving sugar completely is less than the sum of the separate volumes of water and sugar, because dissolved particles occupy the spaces between water particles.
concepts.rule: In Activity 7.6, air trapped inside a syringe with the open end sealed by a thumb can be compressed by pushing the plunger inward, because the gas particles have a lot of space between them in their natural state, and this space can be reduced by applying external pressure; when the plunger is released, the gas particles spread out again and the plunger returns to its original position. Repeating the activity with water instead of air shows that water is practically incompressible. In Activity 7.7, when the level of water in a vessel is marked, sugar is added and a new higher level is marked, and the water is then stirred until the sugar dissolves completely, the resulting water level is lower than the level marked right after adding the sugar; the volume of the solution is less than the sum of the volumes of the water and the sugar, showing there is some space between the water particles, called interparticle spacing, that the dissolved sugar particles come to occupy. Sand, unlike sugar, does not dissolve in water; when sand is added instead, its particles settle down and occupy their own space in the container, so the total volume increases rather than staying close to the original water level. Even in solids, despite the particles being closely packed, some interparticle space is left between them, and this space contains nothing at all, not air.
concepts.example: After sugar is fully dissolved and stirred into water, the final water level is lower than it was right after the sugar was added but before dissolving, showing the dissolved sugar particles have moved into the spaces between the water particles.

concepts.name: Movement of particles: spreading through liquids and gases, and thermal energy
concepts.description: Potassium permanganate spreading through water and fragrance spreading through air show that particles of liquids and gases are in constant motion, faster with more heat; thermal energy decides the physical state of a substance.
concepts.idea: The constant motion of particles makes a coloured substance spread through a liquid and a smell spread through the air, and this motion speeds up with more heat; the thermal energy of particles decides whether a substance behaves as a solid, liquid or gas.
concepts.rule: When a few grains of potassium permanganate are dropped into a glass tumbler of water, pink streaks are first seen spreading out from the grains; with time, the entire bulk of water takes on a uniform pink colour. This happens because the water particles are in constant motion: they first pull particles of potassium permanganate out of the grains, and then hit these particles so that they spread throughout the liquid. Substances like sand are insoluble because their constituent particles are held together too strongly for water particles to pull them out. Repeating this with potassium permanganate dropped into hot water, water at room temperature, and ice-cold water shows that it spreads fastest in hot water, less quickly at room temperature, and slowest in ice-cold water, because water particles move faster when they have more heat energy: the movement of particles increases as heat is provided. In a similar way, when an incense stick is burnt in one corner of a room, its fragrance is felt only nearby at first, but is soon smelled throughout the room, because the particles of air are moving constantly and hit the particles of the fragrance, helping them spread through the room. Bringing these ideas together, the thermal (heat) energy of particles determines the physical state of matter: in the solid state, thermal energy is low, so particles stay close together with strong interparticle attraction and can only vibrate; at the melting point, thermal energy overcomes the attractive forces enough for particles to move away from their fixed positions, with the interparticle distance increasing slightly; in the gaseous state, particles have enough thermal energy to overcome the interparticle attraction almost completely and move freely in all directions. Across the three states, interparticle spacing is minimum in solids, a little more in liquids and maximum in gases; interparticle attraction is maximum in solids, slightly weaker in liquids and minimum (negligible) in gases; and the movement of particles is negligible (only vibrations) in solids, restricted to a limited space in liquids, and spread through all the available space in gases.
concepts.example: A grain of potassium permanganate dropped into hot water colours the whole glass pink faster than the same grain dropped into ice-cold water, because the water particles move faster when they have more heat energy.
